'''''Eucalyptus gomphocephala''''', known as '''tuart''',<ref name="FloraBase" /> is a species of tree and is one of the six forest giants of [[Southwest Australia]].[[File:Eucalyptus gomphocephala frutos.JPG|thumb|Flower buds]][[File:Eucalyptus gomphocephala Tuart Blossom (2347476596).jpg|thumb|Flowers]][[File:Eucalyptus gomphocephala fruit.jpg|thumb|Fruit]] 

The trees usually grow to a height of {{cvt|10|to|40|m}} and mostly have a single stem, but can have multiple stems under some conditions. The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] can be as wide as {{convert|25|m|ft|0}}. It has rough [[Buxus|box]]-like bark over the length of the trunk and larger branches. The glossy light-green to green adult leaves are arranged alternately and have an [[oval]] to [[lanceolate]] or [[Glossary of leaf morphology#Leaf and leaflet shapes|falcate]] shape, and have a leaf blade that is {{convert|90|to|180|mm|in|1}} long and {{cvt|1.5|to|3|cm}} wide. The tree flowers between January and April with white to cream [[inflorescence]]s that form in the leaf [[Glossary of botanical terms#axil|axils]] and are not branched. The fruits that follow have an [[obconic]] to upside-down bell shape.

Tuarts were first formally described by the [[botanist]] [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1828. The botanist [[Jean-Baptiste Leschenault]] assembled the [[Type (biology)|type]] collection at the [[Vasse River]] near [[Geographe Bay]] during 1802, while serving with the [[Baudin expedition to Australia|Baudin expedition]].

The distribution range of tuart is along a narrow coastal corridor within the [[Swan Coastal Plain]], extending inland {{convert|5|to|10|km|mi|1}}, a continuous corridor south from [[Yanchep, Western Australia|Yanchep]] to [[Busselton, Western Australia|Busselton]]. [[Tuart forest]] was common on the Swan coastal plain until the valuable trees were felled for export and displaced by the urban development around [[Perth]]. The wood has many uses as it is dense, hard and water resistant and resists splintering. Remnants of tuart forest occur in state reserves and parks; the tree has occasionally been introduced to other regions of Australia and overseas. Remaining trees are vulnerable to ''[[Phytophthora]]'' dieback, an often fatal disorder. It was listed as [[Endangered species (IUCN status)|endangered]] by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] {{As of|2019|lc=y}}.

==Description==
The tree is native to the southwest of [[Western Australia]] and typically grows to a height of {{convert|10|to|40|m|ft|0}}.<ref name="FloraBase" /> The tallest known living tuart is {{cvt|47|m}} tall and located in the [[Tuart Forest National Park]] near [[Ludlow, Western Australia|Ludlow]]. The largest tuart tree has a wood volume of {{cvt|108|m3|ft3}}.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nicolle |first1=Dean |title=Eucalypts of Western Australia -The South-West Coast and Ranges |date=2019 |publisher=Scott Print |location=WA |isbn=978-0-646-80613-6 |pages=42–43 |edition=1st}}</ref> Taller trees are often found at the southern end of the trees' range, while smaller trees are found at the northern end.<ref name=seed/> The [[Crown (botany)|crown]] of the tree can spread up to a width of {{convert|25|m|ft|0}}.<ref name="camb" /> The [[Habit_(biology)#Structure|habit]] of tuart is a tall single stemmed tree, but may form a low and multi-stemmed tree at the edge of stands in response to salinity and winds.<ref name="Byrne2016">{{cite journal |last1=Byrne |first1=M. |last2=Koenders |first2=A. |last3=Rogerson |first3=K. |last4=Sampson |first4=J. |last5=van Etten |first5=E.J.B. |title=Genetic and morphological analysis of multi-stemmed plants of tuart (''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'') |journal=Australian Journal of Botany |date=2016 |volume=64 |issue=8 |page=704 |doi=10.1071/BT16091 |bibcode=2016AuJB...64..704B }}</ref> The trees have no [[lignotuber]] but will form [[epicormic]] buds up along the stem.<ref name=euclid>{{cite web|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_gomphocephala.htm|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' Tuart|access-date=27 April 2023|work=Euclid|publisher=[[CSIRO]]}}</ref>

Tuart has rough, [[Buxus|box]]-like bark over the length of the trunk and the main branches.<ref name="FloraBase" /><ref name=vicflora>{{cite web|url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/d08558df-d0eb-4ddc-abcb-44770ebeb477|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' DC.|access-date=29 April 2023|work=Flora of Victoria|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria]]|author=Andre Messina|date=9 August 2016}}</ref> The bark is rough and finely fibrous.<ref name=euclid/> It is grey in colour and breaks into smaller flaky pieces.<ref name=camb/><ref name="TBO" /> On large and older stems the bark tends to become [[tessellated]].<ref name=euclid/><ref name=vicflora/> The branchlets have a circular cross-section and often have oil glands situated in the [[pith]], although sometimes there are not many and they can be difficult to find.<ref name=euclid/>

Juvenile leaves are attached to the stem via a stalk and always have an [[Phyllotaxis|opposite]] arrangement for the first four to eight nodes along the [[Plant stem|stem]], then have an alternate arrangement. The green and [[Glossary of botanical terms#discolorous|discolorous]] juvenile leaves have an egg-shaped (ovate) to [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]] shape with a length of {{cvt|9|to|15|cm}} and a width of {{cvt|5.5|to|9.5|cm}}.<ref name=euclid/> Adult leaves are stalked and alternate, with an [[oval]]<ref name="camb" /> to [[lanceolate]] or [[Glossary of leaf morphology#Leaf and leaflet shapes|falcate]] shape. The leaves are slightly discolorous to concolorous, glossy, light green and thin.<ref name=euclid/> The leaf blade is {{convert|90|to|180|mm|in|1}} in length and {{cvt|1.5|to|3|cm}} wide,<ref name=euclid/><ref name="TBO"/> and often curved.<ref name="TBO" /> The leaves are attached to the limbs or [[twig]]s via a [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] that is typically {{cvt|1|to|3|cm}} in length.<ref name=euclid/> The apex of the leaf is pointed and the base tapers to the petiole. Tuart leaves have few oil glands, are densely [[Leaf#Veins|reticulated]], where the veins are packed in tightly forming a dense network in the leaf, and have side veins that branch off at an angle of over 45° to compared to the [[Glossary of botanical terms#midrib|midrib]].<ref name=euclid/>

The tree flowers between January and April and tends to have a mass flowering event every five to eight years with smaller intermittent flowering events for the years in between.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/> White to cream flowers appear in mid-summer to mid-autumn.<ref name="FloraBase" /><ref name=camb/> The [[inflorescence]]s form in the leaf [[Glossary of botanical terms#axil|axils]] and are not branched. The [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] has a length of {{cvt|1|to|3|mm}} with seven buds in each [[umbel]] that are attached by {{cvt|0|to|0.2|cm}} long [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s.<ref name=euclid/> The buds have swollen caps, and are said to resemble a small [[ice cream cone]]; the caps are {{convert|8|to|10|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="TBO" /> The buds are {{cvt|1.5|to|2.4|cm}} in length and have a width of {{cvt|0.9|to|12|cm}} with a hemispherical shaped [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] that is wider than the [[obconic|obconically]] shaped [[hypanthium]] located below. When the outer opercula is shed a scar is left. The stamen are flexed irregularly and contain an oblong [[anther]] that is attached at the rear to the [[filament (botany)|filament]]. The anther can burst open via longitudinal slits. The style is straight and long with a blunt stigma at the tip. The style has a small cavity at the base (or [[locule]]) and holds the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] with four vertical rows of [[ovule]]s.<ref name=euclid/> The flowers are formed in tight clusters made up of around seven flowers. These later form into fruits with a mushroom shape containing small seeds.<ref name=camb/> 

The fruits are narrow and {{convert|1.0|to|2.5|cm|in|2|abbr=on}} in length with a broad rim and {{cvt|1.2|to|1.8|cm}} wide.<ref name="TBO" /><ref name=euclid/> The fruits are attached to the stem via {{cvt|0|to|0.8|cm}} long pedicel. The fruits have an obconic to upside-down bell shape and sometimes have two longitudinal ridges that extend from the pedicel partly along the length. The fruits have a level disc that can be slightly raised or descending and have three to five valves that are partly protruding or exserted.<ref name=euclid/>

The seeds are usually released within a year.<ref name=camb/> They are {{cvt|2|to|3.5|mm}} in length with an ovoid to saucer shape and a grey-brown to blackish colour.<ref name=vicflora/> The upper side of the seed is wrinkled or marked with thin parallel streaks and sometimes has a protruding ridge around the circumference. There is a hilum scar on the rear side where it was once attached to the placenta.<ref name=euclid/> The seeds of this species, as for most ''Eucalypts'', [[germinate]] quite easily and are considered one of the simplest native plants to grow from seed.<ref name=seed/> Seed production has sizable variation throughout time.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/> Seeds are usually slowly released from the canopy but many can be shed at the same time following events such as fire.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/>

== Taxonomy and naming ==
The species was formally described by the [[botanist]] [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in the third volume of his ''[[Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis]]'' 
published in 1828.<ref name="Candolle1828">{{cite book |last1=Candolle |first1=A.P. de |editor1-last=Candolle |editor1-first=A.P. de |editor1-link=A. P. de Candolle |title=Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis |date=1828 |page=220|location=Paris |publisher=Sumptibus Sociorum Treuttel et Würtz  |volume=3 |chapter = Myrtaceae |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/14909/?offset=&height_top=50#page=232&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=}}</ref><ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454645|publisher=APNI|access-date=19 July 2019}}</ref> The botanist [[Jean-Baptiste Leschenault]] assembled the [[Type (biology)|type]] collection at the [[Vasse River]] near [[Geographe Bay]] during 1802,<ref name=gbif_isotype/> while serving with the [[Baudin expedition to Australia|Baudin expedition]].<ref name="Cunningham1998" />

The [[Holotype|isotype]] collected by Leschenault is held at [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref name=gbif_isotype>{{cite journal|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' A.Cunn. ex DC.|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|year=2021|journal=Kew - Herbarium Specimens|doi=10.15468/ly60bx |author1=Jlegind }}</ref>

In 1939, [[William Blakely]] and [[Henry Steedman]] described two varieties of this species in ''Contributions from the New South Wales National Herbarium'', but the names are listed as [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]] by the [[Australian Plant Census]].<ref name="APC" />
The epithet ''gomphocephala'' is derived from ''gomphos'', meaning 'club', and ''kephale'', 'head',<ref name="Ruthrof2002">Ruthrof, K. X., Yates, C. J., & Loneragan, W. A. (2002).  The biology of tuart. In: B. J. Keighhery, V. M. Longman, & W. A. Nedlands (Eds.), ''Tuart (Eucalyptus gomphocephala) and Tuart Communities'' (pp. 108–122). A Perth Branch Wildflower Society of Western Australia.</ref> describing the rounded and overlapping shape of the [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]].<ref name="Sharr1996">{{cite book |title=Western Australian plant names and their meanings: a glossary |date=1996 |editor-first=F.A. |editor-last=Sharr |editor-link= F. A. Sharr |publisher=University of Western Australia Press |isbn=1-875560-43-2 |page=132 |edition=2nd (Enlarged)}}</ref><ref name="TBO" />

The species is allied as a monophyletic arrangement within the most diverse eucalypt subgenus, ''Eucalyptus'' subgen. ''Symphyomyrtus'', recognised as the sole species of its section.<ref name="Ruthrof2002" />

The [[Noongar]] peoples named the tree tuart or ''tooart'', ''moorun'', ''mouarn'' or ''duart''.<ref name="bobhoward" /><ref name=ruthrof_at_al>{{cite web|url=https://researchportal.murdoch.edu.au/esploro/outputs/bookChapter/The-biology-of-Tuart/991005543429707891/filesAndLinks?index=0|title=The biology of tuart|access-date=29 April 2023|author1=Ruthrof, K.X.|author2=Yates, C.J.|author3=Loneragan, W.A.|work=Tuart (Eucalyptus gomphocephala) and Tuart Communities|editor=B. J. Keighery|publisher=[[Murdoch University]]}}</ref>

The tree is sometimes referred to as ''white gum'' and is the origin for the name of the [[Perth, Western Australia|Perth]] suburb [[White Gum Valley, Western Australia|White Gum Valley]].<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/>

==Distribution==
[[File:TuartTree on road reserve near Lake Clifton in 2007 B-W version.png|thumb|Growing on a roadside at [[Lake Clifton, Western Australia|Lake Clifton]], 2007]]
The distribution range of the species is a narrow coastal corridor within the [[Swan Coastal Plain]], extending inland {{convert|5|to|10|km|mi|1}}, a continuous corridor south from [[Yanchep, Western Australia|Yanchep]] to [[Busselton, Western Australia|Busselton]].<ref name="FloraBase" /> This area has been intensively cleared for changes in agricultural practices, then urbanisation, so that the numbers of tuart trees and area of forest were greatly reduced after the establishment of the [[Swan River Colony]].<ref name="Cunningham1998" />
Outlying patches of the tree are found to the north of Yanchep as far as [[Geraldton, Western Australia|Geraldton]] and further inland where rivers intersect the range. The species has become naturalised in other places within Western Australia.<ref name="FloraBase" /> A large stand of Tuart is found adjacent to the [[Jurien Bay, Western Australia|Jurien Bay]] cemetery and is listed with the [[Heritage Council of Western Australia]].<ref name=inherit/><ref name=dcceew/> This stand has scientific value and is regarded as the  "northern most natural Tuart stand in the state". It also has heritage value resulting from its position along an historic [[stock route]].<ref name=inherit>{{cite web|url=https://inherit.dplh.wa.gov.au/public/inventory/printsinglerecord/f5f797bb-8acd-4c4d-9ee5-884efcda0f18|title=Tuart Tree Stand at Jurien Cemetery|access-date=18 December 2023|date=1 January 2017|work=inHerit|publisher=[[Heritage Council of Western Australia]]}}</ref>

Tuarts have been introduced into parts of Europe, specifically in [[Spain]] and [[Italy]] including [[Sicily]]. The species has also been introduced into several countries in Africa, including [[Algeria]], the [[Cape Provinces]] of [[South Africa]], [[Kenya]], [[Libya]], [[Morocco]], [[Tanzania]], [[Tunisia]], [[Zimbabwe]] and the [[Canary Islands]].<ref name=powo>{{cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A592967-1|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' A.Cunn. ex DC.|access-date=27 April 2023|work=[[Plants of the World Online]]|publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]]}}</ref>
The tree has become naturalised in parts of southern Africa.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.biodiversityexplorer.info/plants/myrtaceae/eucalyptus.htm|title=Species naturalised in southern Africa|access-date=9 January 2023|work=biodiversity explorer|publisher=[[Iziko South African Museum]]}}</ref>

''E.{{nbsp}}gomphocephala'' grows in sandy well drained soils, often over [[limestone]],<ref name="FloraBase" /> in sunny positions.<ref name=seed/>

The trees are part of coastal shrubland ecosystems in areas of deep sand. They also will often be part of limited woodland communities in protected areas along the coast.<ref name=camb/> Tuarts are associated with the Quindalup and Spearwood sand dune systems, both of which have [[calcareous]] soils.<ref name=dcceew/> When they occur in woodland or open forest they are often associated with peppermint trees (''[[Agonis flexuosa]]'') in the understorey.<ref name="fpc" />

==Uses==
As a durable [[hardwood]], the [[timber]] is sought after for [[Scantling#Timber and stone|scantlings]], structural timber, the construction of railway carriages and boat building. The colouring and [[grain]] pattern of the timber also make it a popular choice for furniture manufacturing. Due to over-logging, tuart is a protected tree with conditions placed on felling.<ref name=Benara>{{cite web|url=https://www.benaranurseries.com/eucalyptus-gomphocephala|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' Tuart|access-date=15 December 2023|publisher=Benara Nurseries}}</ref><ref name=plantsfuture>{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Eucalyptus+gomphocephala|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' - A.Cunn. ex DC.|access-date=15 December 2023|publisher=Plants For A Future}}</ref>

The heartwood is a pale yellow-brown colour with a fine texture and a highly interlocked grain, close and twisted, almost curled back.<ref name="fpc" /><ref name="Cunningham1998" /> The green wood has a [[density]] of {{convert|1250|kg/m3|lb/ft3|0}} and an air-dried density of {{convert|1030|kg/m3|lb/ft3|0}}.<ref name="fpc" />

The flowers are an excellent source for the production of [[honey]].<ref name="seed" /> The colour of the product is described as light and creamy and it candies quickly to become hard and dry if properly matured in the hive. In 1939, tuart was noted as a high quality source, although it was determined to be an "undependable source" thirty years later.<ref name="Cunningham1998" />

[[Essential oil]]s are extracted from leaves and fruits of the tree. Samples of the leaves contained 0.23% essential oil and samples of the fruits contained 0.34% essential oil. The constituents of the oils collected from the leaves were [[cineole|1,8-cineole]] (24.2%), [[p-cymene]] (20.7%), [[pinene|α-pinene]] (14.1%), β-pinene (8.12%), [[Terpinene|γ-terpinene]] (6.9%),  [[methyleugenol]] (6.8%), [[terpineol|α-terpineol]] (4.7%) and [[limonene]] (3.8%). Essential oil constituents of tuart fruits were 1,8-cineole (46.69 %), p-cymene (8.99 %), baeckeol (8.57 %), α-pinene (5.21 %), and globulol (4.25 %).<ref name=oils>{{cite journal|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0972060X.2020.1727365|title=Chemical Composition and Antimicrobial Activity of Essential Oil from Aerial Part (Leaves and Fruit) of ''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' DC|access-date=28 April 2023|date=6 March 2019|author1=Stanko Stankov|author2=Hafize Fidan|author3=Galina Stefanova|author4=Iliana Kostova|author5=Stanka Damyanova|author6=Ivanka Dimitrova-Dyulgerova|author7=Sezai Ercisli|author8=Albena Stoyanova|journal=Journal of Essential Oil Bearing Plants|volume=23|issue=2|pages=204–212 |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis Online]]|doi=10.1080/0972060X.2020.1727365|s2cid=219411543 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The oils all had some degree of [[antimicrobial]] activity, with the essential oil collected from the leaves generally having higher antimicrobial activity than those collected from the fruit.<ref name=oils/>

== Ecology ==
Tuarts are regarded as one of the six forest giants found in Western Australia; the other trees are ''[[Corymbia calophylla]]'' (marri), ''[[Eucalyptus diversicolor]]'' (karri), ''[[Eucalyptus jacksonii]]'' (red tingle), ''[[Eucalyptus marginata]]'' (jarrah) and ''[[Eucalyptus patens]]'' (yarri).<ref name=seed/><ref name=pfaf>{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/User/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Eucalyptus+gomphocephala|title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala''|access-date=28 April 2023|publisher=Plants For A Future}}</ref> The informal definition of a giant tree is that it must be significantly larger than other species and exceed {{cvt|100|m3}} in volume.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.westernaustraliagianttrees.com/|title=Western Australia Giant Trees|author=Russell Du Guesclin|access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref>

The tree is moderately tolerant of saline soil and salt-laden winds. It is also drought and frost tolerant.<ref name=seed/> 
Individual trees may live over four hundred years.<ref name="Cunningham1998" /><!-- Cunningham1998 -->

[[File:Ludlow forest gnangarra 02.JPG|thumb|[[Tuart Forest National Park|Ludlow forest]]]]
Experimental cultivation in the 1930s of the species identified that it was able to grow in areas of low rainfall, as little as {{convert|13|in}} per annum. Tuarts were introduced to France and grown extensively there by the end of the nineteenth century.<ref name="Cunningham1998" />

The biodiversity of tuart forest is rich, containing unique assemblages of plants, fungi and animals.
A 2009 survey of [[endophytic]] fungi on woody species at two tuart woodlands{{snd}}sampling acacia ''[[Acacia cochlearis]]'', ''[[Acacia rostellifera|A. rostellifera]]'', the sheoak ''[[Allocasuarina fraseriana]]'', peppermint ''[[Agonis flexuosa]]'', ''[[Banksia grandis]]'', sandalwood ''[[Santalum acuminatum]]'' and eucalypts jarrah ''Eucalyptus marginata'' and tuart{{snd}}found around three quarters of isolates were taxa of the family [[Botryosphaeriaceae]]. Eighty percent of these isolates were the species ''[[Neofusicoccum australe]]''. Four new taxa, ''[[Dothiorella moneti]]'', ''[[Dothiorella santali]]'', ''[[Neofusicoccum pennatisporum]]'' and ''[[Aplosporella yalgorensis]]'', resulted from the analysis of the survey. The species ''[[Botryosphaeria dothidea]]'' was also isolated from acacia and jarrah samples.<ref name="Taylor2009" />

Tuart gives its name to a description of an [[ecological community]], as the dominant species of the canopy in [[Tuart forest|tuart woodlands and forests]]. The area where these occur is greatly reduced, and those remaining are fragmented populations of variable quality.<ref name="DEEdraft" /> A proposal submitted in 2017 recommended these be listed as [[critically endangered]] in the nation's register of threatened ecological communities.<ref name="DEEnom" /> Tuart may also occur in the threatened community [[Banksia Woodlands of the Swan Coastal Plain]].<ref name="DEEdraft" />
The Tuart Woodlands and Forests of the Swan Coastal Plain were listed in 2019 as [[critically endangered]] according to the ''[[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]]''.<ref name=dcceew/>

Tuart forest persisted ''in situ'' through the [[Last Glacial Maximum]], and extended its range thirty kilometres to the west as the coastline became exposed by lower sea levels. The historical [[phylogeography]] of the tuart forest indicates the moderating influence of the marine climate in the [[Southwest Australian Floristic Region]] during a period of aridification and other severe climate changes elsewhere on the continent.<ref name="Byrne">{{Citation | author4=[[Stephen Hopper|Hopper, S]]. |author1=Byrne, M. |author2=Coates, D.J. |author3= Forest, F. |author5=Krauss, S.L |author6=Sniderman, J.K.L. |author7= [[Kevin Thiele|Thiele, K.]] |editor=Lambers, Hans| title=Plant life on the sandplains in southwest Australia : a global biodiversity hotspot: kwongan matters | date=2014 | publisher=Crawley, Western Australia UWA Publishing | isbn=978-1-74258-564-2|pages=287–90 |chapter=3. A diverse flora – species and genetic relationships}}</ref>

=== Destructors ===
The insect ''[[Thaumastocoris peregrinus]]'' (bronze bug) is native to the east coast of Australia. The sap-sucking pest has infested non-native ''Eucalyptus'' plantations, including ''E.{{nbsp}}gomphocephala'', in Southern Africa and Europe. Severe infestations of the pest cause leaf loss, leaf senescence, thinning of the canopy and in some cases branch dieback.<ref name=cabi1>{{cite web|url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.109741|title=Thaumastocoris peregrinus (bronze bug)|access-date=28 April 2023|date=22 August 2022|publisher=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International]]|doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.109741 }}</ref>

''[[Phoracantha recurva]]'' (eucalyptus longhorned borer) is another problem pest that can affect newly felled trees or sickly trees found within the native range. It will also attack living trees in areas where it has been introduced, particularly in plantations. It is especially problematic in areas that have a water deficit, where loss of trees in Eucalyptus plantations (particularly ''[[Eucalyptus recurva]]'') is often experienced during [[drought]].<ref name=cabi2>{{cite journal|url=https://plantwiseplusknowledgebank.org/doi/10.1079/pwkb.species.40371|title=Phoracantha recurva (eucalyptus longhorned borer)|journal=Plantwiseplus Knowledge Bank |access-date=29 April 2023|year=2022|volume=Species Pages |article-number=40371 |publisher=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International]]|doi=10.1079/pwkb.species.40371 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Tuart normally release seed gradually and the seeds are open to predation by ants, meaning the [[soil seed bank]] is kept low. Following events such as fire the seeds will be released all at once, this overwhelms the rate of predation and the temporarily increase the soil seed bank.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/>

The species is vulnerable to [[Forest dieback|dieback]] associated with fungal species of the genus ''[[Phytophthora]]''. A study in 2007 of infected or dead tuart trees and woodland identified isolates of ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'', already implicated in the decline of tuart. Another organism ''[[Phytophthora multivora]]'', previously identified as ''[[Phytophthora citricola]]'' complex, was also found and identified.<ref name="Scott2009" />
Damage to reproductive processes by a native predator was first noticed at the end of the nineteenth century. Larvae deposited in flowers by the tuart bud weevil ''[[Haplonyx tibialis]]'' ([[Curculionidae]]) feed on the tissue in the operculum, the female weevil having caused the budding flower to become partly or completely damaged after laying a single egg; the larvae eventually emerge by chewing through the base of the bud.<ref name="Ruthrof2002" />

=== Pollinators ===
Despite no studies having been specifically conducted on ''E{{nbsp}}gomphocephala'', other studies indicate that Eucalypts such as ''[[Eucalyptus muelleriana]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus foecunda]]'' and ''Eucalyptus marginata'', which create smaller cream or white coloured flowers, have smaller volumes of more concentrated nectar and are grouped to produce large [[conflorescence]]s will mostly attract insects. Birds and other animals are attracted to these flowers less often. Eucalypts that produce large flowers with red or yellow coloured filaments such as ''[[Eucalyptus stoatei]]'', ''[[Eucalyptus incrassata]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus rhodantha]]'' and have larger volumes of less concentrated nectar will attract more mammals and birds. These trees tend to attract fewer insects. Applying these ideas it is thought that ''E{{nbsp}}gomphocephala'' is pollinated by insects and birds.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/>
Two species of bird have been recorded  browsing the flowers of ''E{{nbsp}}gomphocephala'': the  [[Lichmera indistincta|brown honeyeater]] and the [[Lichenostomus virescens|singing honeyeater]]. A wide variety of insects have been recorded in mass flowerings of jarrah/tuart woodlands, including 84 different species such as 
ants, bees, wasps, flies, beetles, moths, butterflies and cockroaches.<ref name=ruthrof_at_al/>

== Natural history ==
The extent and maturity of tuart forest and woodland was greatly reduced after colonisation. When [[Charles Fraser (botanist)|Charles Fraser]] viewed tuart trees during a preliminary exploration toward Guildford he remarked on their "stupendous" size.<ref name="Cunningham1998" />
In 1843 [[James Drummond (botanist)|James Drummond]] recorded specimens that were {{cvt|9|to|13|m}} in circumference at a forest north of Busselton.<ref name="Cunningham1998" /><ref name=Ludlow>{{cite web|url=https://www.bdec.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Ludlow-Tuart-Forest-Brochure.pdf|title=Experience the Ludlow Tuart Forest|access-date=17 December 2023|publisher=Busselton-Dunsborough Environmental Centre}}</ref>
[[File:Tuart in Primer of Forestry Poole 1922.png|thumb|Tuart in Lane-Poole's ''Primer of Forestry'' 1927]]
The  [[Swan River Colony]]'s first [[sawmill]] was established in 1833, amongst tuart forest at the foot of Mount Eliza in [[Kings Park, Western Australia|Kings Park]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sites.rootsweb.com/~gregheberle/AdobePDF/Publications/Australia/GregHeberle/TimberhistoryCalmSci-2-3-P204-223.pdf|title=Timber harvesting on Crown Land in the south west of Western Australia|access-date=17 December 2023|year=1991|author=Greg Heberle|publisher=[[Department of Conservation and Land Management (Western Australia)|Department of Conservation and Land Management]]}}</ref> Some of the timber was used by [[Henry Trigg (public servant)|Henry Trigg]] for construction of the new government's infrastructure; Trigg describes the "Tewart" wood's desirable qualities - durable, yet workable - as similar to white gum [eucalypt] and the ''[[lignum vitae]]'' of the South American genus ''[[Guaiacum]]''. 
The four ton cogwheels at the [[Old Mill, Perth]] were hewn from this wood.
The utility of the timber was remarked on by [[George Fletcher Moore]], the 1830s colonial diarist. The value to industries such as shipbuilding was derived from its resistance to splitting and splintering.<!-- Deeplink en:ws --><ref name="Moore 1884">{{cite Q |Q136449801 |last=Moore |first=George Fletcher |author-link=George Fletcher Moore |others=Introduction by [[Tom Stannage|C. T. Stannage]] }}</ref>
The [[British Admiralty]] received loads of this timber at [[Portsmouth]] and [[Chatham Historic Dockyard|Chatham]] during the 1850–60s, exported from [[Wonnerup]] and [[Bunbury, Western Australia|Bunbury]]; an inspection by Thomas Laslett also gave the most favourable possible assessment.<ref name="Maiden1889" />
A plan to export a {{convert|4|m|ft|adj=mid|-wide|spell=in}} tuart to the [[1851 Great Exhibition]] was abandoned when an adequate saw could not be found.
The timber was given additional value due to the proximity of the forests to ports.
The land made available by the destruction of forests was recommended by the state's [[Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (Western Australia)|Department of Agriculture]] in the 1890s for the development of orchards, producing apples, grapes, pears, peaches and nectarines.
The timber produced in the state forest during the early twentieth century was used for railway carriages, greatly reducing costs by replacing steel with tuart and [[wandoo]].<ref name="Lane-Poole1922" /> The wood was only available in small quantities for private uses, notably [[stair tread]]s and the favoured source for [[butcher]]'s blocks.<ref name="Cunningham1998" /><!-- secondary ref to paragraph (N), primary source available (V) -->

The species was surveyed in 1882 by Surveyor General [[Malcolm Fraser (surveyor)|Malcolm Fraser]],<ref name=trouble>{{cite web|url=https://library.dbca.wa.gov.au/static/FullTextFiles/061401.pdf|title=Trouble in the Tuart|access-date=17 December 2023|author=David Ward|publisher=Department of Conservation and Land Management}}</ref> his map showing them occurring at an area measuring {{cvt|130000|ha}}.<!-- Cunningham1998 -->
They were well known to the settlers of the Swan River Colony; the first road from the port to the capital passed through what they named as Claremont Tuart Forest.<!-- Cunningham1998 -->
The first state conservator of forest, [[John Ednie Brown]], reported the remaining extent of tuart forest as {{cvt|81000|ha}} in 1895, and was impressed by straight trunked specimens to {{cvt|50|m}} high and {{cvt|7|m}} circumference, while conceding the density and condition of them prior to his survey were not known to him.
The 1903-04 Royal Commission on Forestry, hearing evidence from sawmiller and government member [[H. J. Yelverton]], reported just over {{cvt|40000|ha}} remained, and that reduced tonnage from areas where "prime trees", those over {{cvt|0.8|m}} in diameter, were mostly harvested had not been found. The conservation of this species was proposed in the commission's summary, emphasising "Tuart is '''the''' most valuable tree …". This eventually took the form of a regulation on export of the tuart, although this was to reserve the timber for its biggest consumer, the state's railway system.<ref name="Cunningham1998" />

When a political means of conserving forest was enacted in 1918, the state conservator [[Charles Lane Poole]]'s recommendation was the purchase of a {{cvt|400|ha}} area near [[Wonnerup]].<ref name=Ludlow/> The State Forest No. 1 was described as "… the last remaining virgin tuart in the world". The State Forest was increased with adjoining areas to around {{cvt|2500|ha}} by 1922,<ref name="Cunningham1998" /> and slightly reduced in 1927 by the conservator [[S. L. Kessel]].<ref name=trouble/> The state sawmill supplying the railway operated in the forest until 1929, using "over mature" trees for the [[covered goods wagon|railway truck]]s being built at the [[Midland Railway Workshops|Midland works]].<ref name="Cunningham1998" />

At the beginning of the twenty first century most of the tuart forest had been felled or cleared. Prior to European settlement the tuart forests occupied an area of {{cvt|125400|ha}} and they now cover an area of {{cvt|17000|ha}}. What remained was recognised as declining in diversity and health of this tree and the assemblages of associated plants, animals and fungi.<ref name=dcceew>{{cite web|url=https://www.dcceew.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/tuart-woodlands-forests-swan-coastal-plain-guide.pdf|title=Tuart Woodlands and Forests of the Swan Coastal Plain: A Nationally Significant Ecological Community|access-date=17 December 2023|year=2019|publisher=[[Department of the Environment and Energy]]}} </ref>

It was listed as [[Endangered species (IUCN status)|endangered]] by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature]] {{As of|2019|lc=y}}.<ref name="iucn status 5 June 2019">{{cite iucn |last1=Fensham |first1=R. |last2=Laffineur |first2=B. |last3=Collingwood |first3=T. |year=2019 |title=''Eucalyptus gomphocephala'' |volume=2019 |article-number=e.T133375329A133375331 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2019-3.RLTS.T133375329A133375331.en |access-date=20 November 2023}}</ref> The species has an estimated [[extent of occurrence]] of {{cvt|19490|km2}} and an estimated [[area of occupancy]] of {{cvt|256|km2}} ranging from [[Jurien, Western Australia|Jurien]] in the north to [[Tuart Forest National Park|Ludlow State Forest]] in the south. The population is declining.<ref name="iucn status 5 June 2019"/>
